title: Two Khalsas, one decision
hookLine: tradition says a split among Sikhs was settled by Bhai Mani Singh casting two slips into the Amritsar pool

lines: NOT A VOTE. NOT A FIGHT.
cards: Two slips of paper, folded small. A pool of still water. A crowd on the steps, everyone watching the surface.

That, tradition says, is how a bitter argument among Sikhs was settled: not by a vote, not by a fight, but by two pieces of paper and a wait. After Banda Singh, Sikhs split over customs some of his followers had taken up.
Both called themselves Khalsa. Both came to Amritsar.

teach.h: A NEW GREETING SPLITS THE PANTH.
teach.b: As tradition tells it, some of Banda Singh's followers had taken up new customs, including a new greeting. Others held that the Guru had given the Khalsa its greeting already, and that nothing should be added.
One side came to be called the Bandai Khalsa. The other called itself the Tat Khalsa, the true or essential Khalsa. Both had fought and suffered.
And when they gathered at Amritsar, the tension was close to breaking into violence.

teach.h: BHAI MANI SINGH PROPOSES A TEST.
teach.b: So Bhai Mani Singh, the respected Sikh caring for the Harmandir, proposed a test that neither side could rig. Tradition says he wrote two greetings on two slips of paper.
On one, the greeting the Bandai Sikhs had taken up.
On the other, the greeting the Khalsa had used since Guru Gobind Singh, the one this path heard again on the day of Chappar Chiri: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh.
Both slips went into the pool together; whichever floated would be accepted, and everyone agreed to the terms before the slips touched the water.
The story says the other slip sank, the Guru's greeting floated, and the matter was settled. Some tellings add more, a wrestling match or a later dispute.
But the heart is the same in each: before the outcome, both sides agreed on how they would decide.
A fair process is a gift to the side that loses.

teach.h: WAHEGURU JI KA KHALSA, WAHEGURU JI KI FATEH.
teach.b: It lets them walk away without being humiliated, and it lets the community stay one community.
Sikhs still greet each other with those words, and the tradition remembers the day a pool of water kept a family from breaking apart.

how: Sikhs greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh," and tell the story of the two slips at Amritsar as part of the history of the Panth after Banda Singh.

games.q: you're Bhai Mani Singh. two sides of the Khalsa are gathered at Amritsar, angry, and close to violence. what do you do?
o: pick the side you think is right and tell the other to leave.
propose a test both sides agree to before anyone knows the result.
send everyone home and avoid the question.
games.why: tradition says he put two slips, one with each greeting, into the pool. both sides agreed first, and the Guru's greeting floated.

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement that is still open, at home or at work, and don't decide who's right.

Instead, ask what fair way of deciding both of you could agree to before you knew the answer: take turns, ask someone neutral, wait a day. Let it take shape, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
